title: Statement on Proposals to Enhance the Transparency and Public Accountability Of the Board's Stress Testing Framework
summary: Fed Governor Michael S. Barr issued a dissenting statement against proposed changes to the Federal Reserve's stress testing framework, arguing that disclosure of models and scenarios would make the tests weaker and less credible. He contends the changes would lead to lower bank capital requirements and increased gaming risks, potentially leaving banks in a worse position to weather stress.
key_points: Barr opposes the package of changes to the supervisory stress test, arguing model and scenario disclosure will reduce test rigor and lead to 'ossification'
The proposed changes could create a 'one-way ratchet' on capital requirements as banks object to aspects producing higher requirements
Banks may shift to riskier assets where disclosed models underestimate risks, and engage in window dressing and strategic hedging to game the tests
If the new credit, market, and operational risk models had been used for 2024 or 2025 tests, projected capital ratios would have been roughly 100 basis points higher (~$115 billion)

The proposal reduces risk sensitivity and conservatism in modeling—for example, mortgage loss projections have fewer non-linear effects, probability of default assumptions are less conservative, and operational risk is no longer macro-sensitive
The PPNR model reliance on banking industry estimates of noninterest income and expense may incentivize banks to make rosier estimates, biasing models over time
The proposed 2026 scenario is described as at the 'low end of stressfulness' compared to prior tests
why_it_matters: This statement reveals significant disagreement within the Fed about stress test methodology. The proposed changes could materially lower capital requirements for large banks and reduce the resilience of the banking system. Banks' ability to game tests using newly disclosed model details could create hidden risks, and reduced management buffers would leave banks more vulnerable in actual stress events. The potential for 'model monoculture' could also create concentration risks in certain assets.
market_structure_context: This statement directly addresses market structure through its focus on bank capital adequacy, stress testing methodology, and the potential for gaming in regulatory frameworks. It highlights how model disclosure could alter bank behavior and risk selection, potentially creating new concentration risks. The proposed changes to credit, market, and operational risk models would reduce risk sensitivity and conservatism in how the Fed models bank stress.

$115 billion — estimated additional capital more optimistically projected under the new three models
